Issued at 355 AM CDT Mon Aug 3 2026

Mid and upper-level ridge axis is still present from the Kansas High 
Plains into Upper Midwest this morning, but upstream we are seeing 
signs of deamplification as a stronger short-wave trough exits the 
Pacific Northwest and heads for the Northern Plains and Canadian 
Prairie Provinces. The stronger dAVA over the lower Missouri River 
Valley the past few days has shifted toward the Ohio River Valley 
and Tennessee Valley, and has forced the surface anticyclone center 
eastward. Multiple short-wave perturbations over the Rockies has 
provided enough dCVA and lift that has resulted in surface 
cyclogenesis, with recent objective analysis having this centered 
over eastern Wyoming this morning. The stronger mid-level support 
will start to shift northeastward into the Northern Plains, which 
will limit surface pressure falls for the forecast area, at least 
for today. However the 594dam H5 high over the desert southwest is 
also expected to deamplify over the next 24 hours. Expecting short-
wave activity to generate cyclonic vorticity into Colorado and the 
Front Range through the evening, providing another area of surface 
pressure falls which will extend southward from the cyclone 
currently deepening over Wyoming. For the lower Missouri River 
Valley, this sets lower tropospheric flow southwesterly, increasing 
the strength of WAA this afternoon and will help boost temperatures 
into the upper 80s across most of the areas, and a few locations may 
potentially hit the 90F mark this afternoon. Moisture return today 
will be fairly modest, and without any stronger mid-level lift over 
the area, should help keep conditions dry for today. Western 
Missouri and eastern Kansas may see an uptick in winds later in the 
afternoon, but the stronger pressure gradient remains progged over 
the Central Plains. 

Tuesday, short-wave H5 trough moves a stronger lobe of vorticity 
across the northern Plains, with mid-level height falls deamplifying 
the ridge axis across the area. Additional mid-level vorticity 
generates over the Rockies in Colorado, and this dCVA will help 
promote surface pressure falls from the Front Range to the Central 
Plains, while the cyclone over eastern Wyoming moves into the 
northern Plains along with the primary short-wave trough axis. This 
movement will also push a cold front into the Central Plains through 
most of Tuesday afternoon. During this time in the afternoon, most 
of the forcing remains well west and northwest of the forecast area. 
However, flow from 850mb to the surface will become more southerly 
through the afternoon, transporting a higher theta-e airmass into 
the lower Missouri River Valley. Expecting temperatures to hit the 
90s across much of the area, with steadily increasing dewpoints. The 
afternoon still looks to remain dry for most of the area, but as the 
cold front moves east-southeast along surface pressure falls 
spreading across the Plains, convergence will increase eventually 
bringing providing the lift needed for shower activity. Current 
ensemble guidance pinpoints the highest probabilities for rain showers 
in northern Missouri by late Tuesday Night. If there is enough CAPE, 
a few rumbles of thunder may occur with this activity. The stronger 
deep layer shear on Tuesday should remain over the central Plains, 
which will limit the ability for activity to organize on Tuesday in 
far northern Missouri. 

Wednesday, another short-wave trough and enhanced mid-level vort max 
is currently progged to dig further south, especially in the GFS 
solution which will provide more lift along with the surface cyclone 
and cold front moving toward the area. With continued south and 
southeasterly flow near the surface, theta-e transport will 
continue, and as the day progresses should see shower activity 
spread across most of the forecast area. With the stronger mid-level 
flow on Wednesday afternoon and evening, deep layer shear values 
increase, with 0-6km bulk shear values potentially hitting near 40kt 
especially close to thermal boundary. This will provide the support 
needed to help storm activity organize, and may help produce 
stronger to marginally severe storms. This morning's SWODY3 outlook 
places much of the area in a marginal risk (level 1 of 5). The 
source of uncertainty is how much destabilization will be able to 
occur Wednesday afternoon and early evening. With a lot of activity 
expected over the Plains, we may end of with mid and upper-level 
cloud cover, limiting insolation and the ability for the boundary 
layer to destabilize. In addition, with deeper moisture transport, 
model soundings are not showing any kind of EML development, 
therefore, keeping lapse rates marginal as the forcing move through 
the area on Wednesday. If stronger updrafts are able to develop, a 
few severe wind gusts would be the primary threat, along hail around
